newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Power cuts, shortages bite in Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: Power cuts, shortages bite in Sierra Leone.

text.p: Power cuts and food shortages are biting hard in Sierra Leone as West African neighbours demanding reinstatement of ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah tighten an economic blockade.

With talks pending, a clandestine radio station loyal to Kabbah said that a Nigerian-led West African force was still enforcing a land, sea and air blockade -- including oil supplies for the main power station.
"Because of the lack of fuel, the Ministry of Energy and Power has been forced to embark on providing electricity mainly for priority locations," one source close to the ministry said.
The source listed state radio and television, key military installations, state hospitals and main government offices.
One ministry source said the country was running on its "last drops of fuel". Residents say parts of the capital Freetown, especially the east, have gone days without power.

Young soldiers toppled Kabbah on May 25, accusing him of blocking peace with rebels and humiliating the army by giving special status to a traditional hunter militia. Rebels, who took up arms in 1991, rallied to the coup.
West African foreign ministers agreed in neighbouring Guinea on June 26 that they would seek the return of Kabbah through dialogue and sanctions but also retained the military option.
The West African force, called ECOMOG, is in Sierra Leone under a pre-coup defence pact.

The pro-Kabbah radio, whose broadcasts sparked a clash between Nigerian troops and Sierra Leone soldiers and rebels hunting for the transmitter, said ECOMOG commanders had warned ships and planes to stay away.
Peace talks in Ivory Coast on July 18 between the ruling military junta and West African foreign ministers ended with a statement that all hostilities should end.
Junta officials interpreted that as bringing an end to the blockade that has pushed up prices of scarce foodstuffs.
Talks are planned for Tuesday in Ivory Coast.
Nigerian troops have allowed food trucks into the capital, but ECOMOG officials have said the blockade is still in place.
Residents say the cost of a bag of rice in Freetown has doubled to 40,000 leones ($50) from 20,000 on the eve of the May 25 coup. It is even higher in the provincial towns, they added.
State radio, under the junta's control, has warned traders not to charge more than 25,000 leones a bag for rice, a staple food in Sierra Leone, and has said a shipload was on its way.

The sole remaining rice importer in Sierra Leone, Alhaji Hassan Bazzy, told the Quill newspaper on Saturday that a Russian-registered ship was in neighbouring Guinea, but was due to reach Freetown on Sunday with 136,000 bags.
Asked if the blockade was preventing shipments, he replied that high freight insurance costs caused by the conflict were the main problem.
Outside the capital, ministry sources say Bo and Kenema in the south and east have power from the Dodo hydroelectric dam.
Poor upkeep of power generating units and lack of fuel caused pre-coup problems in the north, where main towns Makeni and Kabala have been without all electricity since the coup.

In Freetown, truck and car drivers queue for days for fuel. Black market prices have soared. Residents say lack of fuel has forced fishing boats to stay in port -- sending the price of fish soaring -- and the price of candles has doubled.
($1 = 800 leones)
